title: Brain implant at the University of California, San Francisco, decodes a woman's attempted speech at 78 words per minute 18 years after a stroke, and the implant is removed in February 2024 for an unrelated reason
summary: A speech neuroprosthesis built at the University of California, San Francisco, decoded Ann Johnson's attempted speech into text at a median 78 words per minute and drove a voice and an avatar.
account: In 2005 a pontine infarct left a woman with quadriplegia and anarthria. News reports name her Ann Johnson. She had communicated by letterboard, and the paper reports that her usual head-tracking device gave about 14.2 words per minute. At 47 she took part in the BRAVO trial (NCT03698149) at the medical center of the University of California, San Francisco. In September 2022 a 253-channel electrocorticography array was implanted over her speech cortical areas. Deep-learning recurrent neural networks trained on her attempted silent speech decoded text at a median 78 words per minute. Median word error rate was 25% over a 1,024-word vocabulary. The networks also synthesized speech personalized to her pre-injury voice and animated a facial avatar. The paper ties the text-decoding result to 14 days of data collection shortly after the September 2022 implant and gives no calendar session dates. Metzger and colleagues reported the results in Nature on 23 August 2023. In a Nature commentary of the same day, Nick Ramsey and Nathan Crone, who were not part of the study, called this result and Stanford's a turning point for restoring communication. In February 2024 her implant was removed for a reason unrelated to the trial. She took part in a streaming-synthesis study published in 2025, whose data predate the removal. On 13 August 2025 Berkeley News reported the removal. It also reported that she still writes to the team with her current assistive technology.
purpose: Built to restore communication by decoding attempted speech from cortical surface recordings into text, synthesized speech and avatar animation. That was the intended benefit and is what occurred.
model_version: 253-channel high-density ECoG array; bidirectional RNN decoders with CTC loss producing text, synthesized speech and avatar gestures; 1,024-word vocabulary
developer: UCSF Chang Lab with UC Berkeley

ratings.reason: One identifiable person communicated by decoded text, a synthesized voice and an avatar in research sessions at her residence. The paper reports no independent use outside those sessions. Her implant was removed in February 2024.

ai_role.statement: Deep-learning decoders are the mechanism. They map cortical activity during attempted speech to phonemes, speech units and articulatory gestures, and every output (text, voice, avatar) depends on them.

fields.summary: A speech neuroprosthesis built at the University of California, San Francisco, decoded Ann Johnson's attempted speech into text at a median 78 words per minute and drove a voice and an avatar.
fields.account: In 2005 a pontine infarct left a woman with quadriplegia and anarthria. News reports name her Ann Johnson. She had communicated by letterboard, and the paper reports that her usual head-tracking device gave about 14.2 words per minute. At 47 she took part in the BRAVO trial (NCT03698149) at the medical center of the University of California, San Francisco. In September 2022 a 253-channel electrocorticography array was implanted over her speech cortical areas. Deep-learning recurrent neural networks trained on her attempted silent speech decoded text at a median 78 words per minute. Median word error rate was 25% over a 1,024-word vocabulary. The networks also synthesized speech personalized to her pre-injury voice and animated a facial avatar. The paper ties the text-decoding result to 14 days of data collection shortly after the September 2022 implant and gives no calendar session dates. Metzger and colleagues reported the results in Nature on 23 August 2023. In a Nature commentary of the same day, Nick Ramsey and Nathan Crone, who were not part of the study, called this result and Stanford's a turning point for restoring communication. In February 2024 her implant was removed for a reason unrelated to the trial. She took part in a streaming-synthesis study published in 2025, whose data predate the removal. On 13 August 2025 Berkeley News reported the removal. It also reported that she still writes to the team with her current assistive technology.
